item.title: Himeji Yukata Festival: The Season's First Summer Robes — Guide
item.description: The Himeji Yukata Festival, held over three nights each June, is one of the oldest and largest summer events in western Japan and traditionally the first occasion of the year for wearing a yukata. It began in the eighteenth century, when a newly arrived lord dedicated a shrine and, so the story goes, told townspeople who had no formal dress to come in their light cotton robes instead. Today several hundred thousand people fill the streets below Himeji Castle over three evenings, among hundreds of food stalls, shrine rites and lantern-lit lanes.

item.title: Kinosaki Onsen: The Willow-Lined Hot Spring Town — Guide
item.description: Kinosaki Onsen, on the Sea of Japan coast of northern Hyogo, is the most complete and atmospheric hot spring town in the country. A willow-lined canal runs through its centre, crossed by little stone bridges and flanked by wooden inns, and the whole town is built around a single idea: guests stay in a ryokan but bathe out in the town, wandering between seven public bathhouses in yukata and clattering wooden geta.

item.title: Kyoto Kimono Rental Guide: Dressing the Part in the Old Capital
item.description: There is no more atmospheric way to explore Kyoto’s historic streets than dressed in a kimono. As you walk the stone lanes of Higashiyama or cross a bridge in Arashiyama, the traditional silhouette transforms the experience — and the photographs. Kimono rental in Kyoto is easy, affordable, and hugely popular with visitors of every nationality and gender: shops dress you head to toe, style your hair, and send you out for the day.

item.title: Sumida River Fireworks Guide: Tokyo's Greatest Summer Spectacle
item.description: The Sumida River Fireworks Festival (隅田川花火大会, Sumidagawa Hanabi Taikai) is the oldest and most prestigious fireworks festival in Tokyo, with roots tracing back to 1733. Over 20,000 shells launch across two competing sites along the Sumida River on the last Saturday of July, watched by roughly one million spectators packed onto bridges, riverbanks, rooftops, and into restaurants for miles around. It is one of the definitive Tokyo summer experiences — and also one of the most logistically demanding to attend well.
